final_answer: No. The trial court did not err (and almost certainly did not abuse its discretion) in disqualifying Smith Fullingham. Disqualification is reviewed for abuse of discretion, and mandamus is available to review it. Texas applies a two-step presumption for a nonlawyer (legal assistant or paralegal) who switches sides. (1) Irrebuttable presumption: a nonlawyer who worked on a matter for one side is conclusively presumed to have obtained that client's confidences. Jones's work satisfies this. She prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications, and attended strategy meetings on this very suit. Her claimed lack of memory does not matter. (2) Rebuttable presumption: the nonlawyer is presumed to have shared those confidences with the new firm. The firm can rebut this only by effective screening. Phoenix Founders, Inc. v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994); National Medical Professional Corp. v. Godbey, 924 S.W.2d 123 (Tex. 1996); In re American Home Products Corp., 985 S.W.2d 68 (Tex. 1998); In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, L.P., 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010). The firm cannot rebut here. Columbia Valley holds that disqualification is always required when confidential information has in fact been disclosed, or when screening would be ineffective or the nonlawyer necessarily would have to work on the other side of the same or a substantially related matter. Screening must be timely, meaning in place when the nonlawyer joins the firm, and the Court looks at the timing and features of the measures taken. Here the matter is the same, so the substantial-relationship element is met. The firm did no conflict inquiry in 2017 and imposed no screen until 2023, six years after she arrived. During that time she actually worked on the Apex-Prestige dispute on thirteen occasions and e-filed two documents in March 2022 under her own name. A screen adopted after she had already worked on the same matter on the opposing side is not timely and cannot cure the conflict. The firm's responses that she does not recall the work and shared nothing are inadequate. The first is irrelevant under the irrebuttable presumption. The second is a bare denial. Texas courts do not require the former client to prove actual disclosure, because that would force it to reveal the confidences it seeks to protect, and the Court has said that an affidavit of non-disclosure alone does not rebut the presumption. The firm also has the practical burden because it failed to screen when she joined. The firm may argue that Owens Farmer withdrew in 2011, that her work was limited and secretarial, and that Apex waited. None of this succeeds. A prior firm's withdrawal does not end the duty of confidentiality to the former client, and the same-matter relationship continues through the 2017 remand and the new trial. Her work for the firm was on the same matter, which is the circumstance Phoenix Founders and Columbia Valley identify as requiring disqualification, and her role was not trivial. Waiver by delay requires unreasonable delay after the movant knows of the conflict (see, e.g., In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998), and In re Users System Services, 22 S.W.3d 331 (Tex. 1999), as I recall them; not verified in this run). Apex learned in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023, a few weeks later, which is not unreasonable. Disqualification is a severe remedy and movants must show actual prejudice (In re Nitla, 92 S.W.3d 419 (Tex. 2002)); the ethical rules are guidelines, not controlling standards. Prejudice is shown here because the firm's side had a paralegal with knowledge of Apex's privileged strategy on a matter heading to retrial. The Texas Disciplinary Rules, Rule 5.03, on supervising nonlawyer assistants, support this result as persuasive guidance, though the Texas Supreme Court has said they do not govern disqualification. Caveat: I verified only Columbia Valley's holding through a secondary search summary; the other citations are from memory and were not independently verified in this run. Result: affirm disqualification of Smith Fullingham.
